title: Classifiers: counting things the right way
title_target: ລັກສະນະນາມ — Lak-sa-na-náam
goal: Count anything with the right classifier, order quantities at food stalls and shops, and point out "this one, that one" without naming the thing.
bekal: the most common classifiers: ຄົນ ໂຕ ອັນ ໜ່ວຍ ໃບ ຫົວ
ask how many with ຈັກ + classifier
use ອັນນີ້ / ອັນນັ້ນ in place of a noun

dialogs.title: ບົດສົນທະນາ — At the corner grocery store
dialogs.intro: Budi is shopping for everyday things. Count how many times a classifier appears in this dialogue — Lao almost never says a number without one.

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ສະບາຍດີ|Sa-baai-dii] [ມີ|Míi][ນ້ຳ|nâm][ບໍ່|bàw]

lines.speaker: ຄົນຂາຍ:
lines.text: [ມີ|Míi] [ເອົາ|Ao][ຈັກ|ják][ຂວດ|khùat]

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ສາມ|Sǎam][ຂວດ|khùat] [ແລ້ວ|Lèeo][ກໍ|kaw][ເບຍ|bia][ສອງ|sǎwng][ຂວດ|khùat][ນຳ|nám]
lines.id: Three bottles. And two bottles of beer too.
lines.literal: three — bottle. then — also — beer — two — bottle — along.

lines.speaker: ຄົນຂາຍ:
lines.text: [ໄດ້|Dâi] [ເອົາ|Ao][ຫຍັງ|nyǎng][ອີກ|ìik][ບໍ່|bàw]

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ຂໍ|Khǎw][ໄຂ່|khài][ສິບ|síp][ໜ່ວຍ|nùay] [ແລະ|Lae][ເຂົ້າໜົມ|khào-nǒm][ຖົງ|thǒng][ໜຶ່ງ|nʉ̀ng]
lines.id: Ten eggs, please, and a bag of snacks.
lines.literal: ask-for — egg — ten — piece. and — snack — bag — one.

lines.speaker: ຄົນຂາຍ:
lines.text: [ເຂົ້າໜົມ|Khào-nǒm][ອັນ|an][ໃດ|dai] [ອັນ|An][ນີ້|nîi][ຫຼື|lʉ̌ʉ][ອັນ|an][ນັ້ນ|nân]
lines.id: Which snacks? This one or that one?
lines.literal: snack — piece — which? piece — this — or — piece — that?

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ອັນ|An][ນັ້ນ|nân] [ອັນ|An][ສີ|sǐi][ຂຽວ|khǐao]

lines.speaker: ຄົນຂາຍ:
lines.text: [ໄດ້|Dâi] [ໝົດ|Mót][ຫ້າ|hāa][ສິບ|síp][ພັນ|phán][ກີບ|kìip]
lines.id: Okay. That's fifty thousand kip altogether.
lines.literal: can. used-up — five — ten — thousand — kip.

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ນີ້|Nîi][ເດີ້|dòe] [ຂ້ອຍ|Khàwy][ບໍ່|bàw][ມີ|míi][ຖົງ|thǒng] [ຂໍ|Khǎw][ຖົງ|thǒng][ໜຶ່ງ|nʉ̀ng][ໃບ|bai][ໄດ້|dâi][ບໍ່|bàw]
lines.id: Here you go. I didn't bring a bag. Could I have one?
lines.literal: this — (friendly). I — not — have — bag. ask-for — bag — one — sheet — can — (question)?

lines.speaker: ຄົນຂາຍ:
lines.text: [ໄດ້|Dâi][ເລີຍ|lóei] [ຂອບໃຈ|Khàwp-jai][ເດີ້|dòe]

notes: **The order is always: noun + number + classifier.** *ນ້ຳສາມຂວດ nâm sǎam khùat* = "water three bottle." English puts the number first ("three bottles of water"); Lao puts it after the noun. The wrong order is still understood, but it sounds instantly foreign.

**For "one," the number moves AFTER the classifier.** *ຖົງໜຶ່ງ thǒng nʉ̀ng* (one bag) sounds natural; *ໜຶ່ງຖົງ* sounds like reading a list. It's a habit, not a hard rule — but follow it, because everyone does.

**ຈັກ ják + classifier = "how many."** *ຈັກຂວດ* (how many bottles), *ຈັກຄົນ* (how many people), *ຈັກໜ່ວຍ* (how many pieces). Notice that the classifier must still appear even though the number isn't known yet.

**ອັນ an is the emergency classifier.** It's used for small things with no special classifier — and if you forget the right one, *ອັນ* is almost always accepted. It also works as a pronoun for things: *ອັນນີ້* (this one), *ອັນນັ້ນ* (that one), *ອັນໃດ* (which one).

**A classifier can stand alone without the noun**, as long as both sides know what's meant. *ເອົາສອງໂຕ* (I'll take two of them), *ເອົາອັນສີຂຽວ* (I'll take the green one). This is what makes Lao conversation sound so compact.

**ຂໍ khǎw = "to ask for," and it's the most polite way to start a request.** *ຂໍນ້ຳແດ່* (some water, please), *ຂໍເບິ່ງແດ່* (may I have a look). Compare *ເອົາ ao*, which is more like "take" — fine at stalls and shops, but too direct for asking a favor.
**ໝົດ mót means "used up," and it's used for "in total."** *ໝົດຫ້າສິບພັນ* = "fifty thousand altogether." The same word means "sold out": *ໝົດແລ້ວ* (all gone).

**ກໍ kaw = "also, then."** It comes before the verb and links the sentence to the one before: *ແລ້ວກໍເອົາເບຍນຳ* (and then beer too). Together with *ນຳ nám* (along, too) at the end, it's the most common way to add something.

*ໄຂ່ສິບໜ່ວຍ* — ten eggs
*ປີ້ໜຶ່ງໃບ* — one ticket
*ປຶ້ມສອງຫົວ* — two books
*ລົດສາມຄັນ* — three cars
*ນ້ຳສາມຂວດ* — three bottles of water
*ນ້ຳສອງແກ້ວ* — two glasses of water
*ກາເຟຈອກໜຶ່ງ* — a cup of coffee

after: Don't memorize the whole table today. Take the first six; the rest will stick through use, and *ອັນ* covers everything you haven't learned yet.

grammars.title: Pointing without naming the thing
body: Classifier + demonstrative makes a complete pronoun for things. You'll use it constantly in shops and at food stalls.

head: Lao
Say it
Meaning
When
rows: something far from both of you

after: ⚠️ Lao distinguishes **three distances**, not two: *ນີ້* (near me), *ນັ້ນ* (near you), *ພຸ້ນ* (far from both of us). Modern English uses "that" for the last two — older English had "yonder" for the third.

sections.title: Everyday shopping items and their classifiers

blocks.text: Notice **ເຂົ້າ *khào*** (rice) and **ເຂົ້າໜົມ *khào-nǒm*** (snack): they share a word because both are made from rice. In Laos, "rice" almost always means **ເຂົ້າໜຽວ *khào-nǐao*** — sticky rice, eaten by hand from a woven basket. Regular rice is *ເຂົ້າຈ້າວ khào-jâao*.

Notice that many color names are **a thing + its color**, much like English "orange" or "sky blue": *ສີນ້ຳຕານ* is literally "sugar-water color" (brown), *ສີບົວ* "lotus color" (pink), *ສີຟ້າ* "sky color." The word *ສີ sǐi* in front can be dropped when it's clear: *ເສື້ອແດງ sʉ̂a deeng* (red shirt).
